design_detail: Short report from the South Atlantic Fentanyl Test Strip Study (SAFTSS): a three-wave prospective cohort of people who inject drugs recruited at two syringe services programmes in rural west-central North Carolina (Appalachian foothills) and north-central West Virginia, baseline June 2021 to March 2022, with follow-up surveys at 6 and 12 months; it extends the baseline report (Zibbell et al., 2024; not read). Outcome: self-reported past-30-day fentanyl test strip (FTS) use at each wave, modelled with mixed-effects logistic regression (subject-specific random intercept) on survey wave, time-invariant covariates and time-varying characteristics, in all 541 baseline participants (1081 observations) and in the 212 who completed both follow-ups (636 observations), with gender-interaction models. FTS use is the outcome here, not an intervention given or compared, so ROBINS-E is used (exposures: witnessing an overdose, housing, drug use, opioid preference) rather than ROBINS-I; the decline across waves is a within-cohort trend, appraised for attrition and for changes over calendar time.
can_establish: Whether self-reported past-30-day fentanyl test strip use changed over 12 months in a cohort of rural people who inject drugs attending two syringe services programmes, recruited in 2021–2022, and which characteristics (witnessing an overdose, being unhoused, heroin use, marital status) were associated with use.
cannot_establish: Why use fell (fentanyl saturation of the market, test-strip supply, contact with services and perceived risk were not measured), whether witnessing an overdose motivates testing (a self-reported association open to confounding by service contact), whether testing changed behaviour or prevented overdose (not studied), or how common use was at each wave (not given in the main text).

sample.recruitment: Community: purposive recruitment by direct intercept of people receiving services at two syringe services programmes, one in North Carolina and one in West Virginia (Olive Branch Ministry and Milan Puskar Health Right, named in the acknowledgements) (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2; Acknowledgments, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older, injected drugs in the past 30 days, proficient in English and willing to share contact information for follow-up (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2). No exclusions are reported.
sample.demographics: Full sample at baseline (Table 1, p. 2): mean age 38.8 (SD 9.5); 210 women (38.8%); 98 non-White (18.1%); 168 (31.1%) recruited in West Virginia; 390 (72.1%) with a high school degree; 102 (18.9%) married or living as married; 288 (53.2%) currently unhoused; past-30-day use of methamphetamine 466 (86.1%), heroin 384 (71%) and fentanyl 247 (45.7%). For the complete-case sample the text gives 69% North Carolina, 39% women, 91% non-Hispanic White, 69% at least a high school education and 60% unhoused (Results › Descriptive findings, 1st paragraph), which conflicts with Table 1 on race and education (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Of 541, 328 (60.6%) completed at least one follow-up and 212 (39.2%) both; 213 (39.4%) had no follow-up (editors' percentages). Compared with the complete-case sample, the 213 without follow-up had less often witnessed an overdose (56.8% against 69.8%) and less often used FTS (54.3% against 65.1%, lifetime use at baseline), and were less likely to be married (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 3); the same phrase also lists being unhoused (read literally, also less likely), without figures. Attrition statistics are in the supplement (not read).
sample.selection_effects: A convenience sample of people already in contact with two rural syringe services programmes; how participants obtained test strips, and whether supply changed during follow-up, is not described. People outside services are not represented. Follow-up retained people more engaged with harm reduction (more lifetime FTS use, more witnessed overdoses), which may bias the trend and the associations. The authors note that findings may not generalise beyond the two programmes or beyond participants who stayed engaged (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 3).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported at each survey wave (survey mode not stated in this report): past-6-month witnessing of an overdose and own overdose; current housing; past-30-day use (yes or no) of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, crack and powder cocaine; injections per day; preference for heroin or fentanyl; access to heroin not containing fentanyl; plus sex, age, race/ethnicity, high school degree, marital status, state and enrolment quarter (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2; Table 1). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Injection drug use in the past 30 days was an eligibility criterion; mean injections per day at baseline 5.6 (SD 8) in the full sample (Table 1). Reported as study characteristics only.
exposure.polysubstance: Past-30-day use of methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, crack and powder cocaine entered the model as separate time-varying covariates; 86.1% reported methamphetamine use at baseline (Table 1). Whether drugs reported as heroin contained fentanyl was not tested; the authors suggest some participants may wrongly believe they use heroin (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 3).

comparison.controls: No unexposed control group. Comparisons are between survey waves within the cohort and between participants with and without each characteristic, all entered in one model.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured or not reported: how often participants used the syringe services programmes and whether they were given test strips during follow-up; perceived risk of fentanyl and reasons for testing or not testing; social networks; mental health; what participants' drugs contained. The authors' explanations (fentanyl saturation, perceived risk of adulteration) rest on variables that are not in the model.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported past-30-day FTS use (yes or no) at baseline, 6 and 12 months; lifetime FTS use is also given descriptively for complete cases (Results › Descriptive findings, 3rd paragraph, pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: A single self-reported item, not verified; the survey instrument is not described in this report (the baseline paper, not read, describes the survey).
outcomes.operationalization: Any FTS use in the past 30 days. How often people tested, what results they got and what they did after a result were not analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; about 19 coefficients per model in two samples, plus gender-interaction models from which three significant differences are reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios from mixed-effects logistic regression, full sample then complete cases (Table 1, p. 2): 12-month wave 0.642 (95% CI 0.447–0.923) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853); 6-month wave 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375); witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months 2.444 (1.784–3.347) and 2.257 (1.529–3.334); currently unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913) and 0.611 (0.410–0.909); past-30-day heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357) and 1.891 (1.178–3.036); married or living as married 1.521 (1.084–2.134) and 1.608 (1.073–2.410); enrolment quarter 0.793 (0.674–0.932) and 0.825 (0.670–1.015); preferring fentanyl over heroin 0.775 (0.564–1.067) and 0.662 (0.440–0.996); own overdose 0.981 (0.676–1.424) and 0.712 (0.416–1.218). The odds ratios are conditional on the random intercept; no predicted probabilities or wave-specific percentages of past-30-day use are printed in the main text, and the gender-interaction estimates are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.covariates: Survey wave; sex, age, race/ethnicity, high school degree, marital status and state; enrolment quarter (in Table 1, not in the Methods list); time-varying housing, past-30-day use of five drugs, injections per day, own and witnessed overdose, opioid preference and access to heroin without fentanyl, all in one model (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The prevalence of the primary outcome at each wave, the gender-interaction estimates and the attrition statistics are not in the main text (supplement not read). The Methods say Table 1 shows the direction and significance of the stratified results, which it does not.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation is reported; several intervals in the complete-case sample are wide (for example non-White 0.270–1.337).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 541 rural people who inject drugs, the odds of past-30-day FTS use were lower at 12 months than at baseline (aOR 0.642; complete cases 0.557) but not at 6 months (0.936; 0.946). Witnessing an overdose (2.444; 2.257), heroin use (1.615; 1.891) and being married were associated with higher odds, and being unhoused with lower odds (0.679; 0.611); own overdose, fentanyl use and access to heroin were not associated. Lifetime FTS use among complete cases rose from 65.1% to 79.7%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes on “declines in FTS use amongst the SAFTSS cohort at six and 12 months” (p. 1), but the 6-month odds ratios are close to 1 with intervals including 1. It calls direct exposure to overdose a key motivator for engaging with harm reduction (p. 1), a causal reading of a self-reported association that could equally reflect contact with services, social networks or reverse ordering. The Discussion describes a decline across all demographic groups (only gender was examined), attributes it to the reduced value of testing for fentanyl in a fentanyl-saturated market rather than to unwillingness, and says FTS use is driven by perceived risk of adulteration (p. 3): reasons for testing and perceived risk were not measured.

timeline.event: Krieger et al.: cited for FTS prompting risk reduction such as using less and not using alone; not read.
Peiper et al., an earlier North Carolina study with the last author: cited for five-fold higher odds of safer use after a positive result; not read.
SAFTSS baseline data collection, June 2021 to March 2022.

Zibbell et al.: SAFTSS baseline findings from the same cohort, cited for fentanyl exposure being broadly presumed; not read. Kutscher et al. (2024), a scoping review read for this batch, relays documented FTS use of 1–80% (median 19%) across studies and more frequent use of drug checking among people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months (one study).

replication.where_it_stands: No independent longitudinal estimate of FTS use over time was found among the papers read for this batch; the baseline report comes from the same cohort and authors and is not a replication. The association with witnessing an overdose agrees in direction with the one study relayed by Kutscher et al. (2024).

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse: R01DA046444 (Dr. Zibbell, PI) and R01DA047334 (Drs. Zibbell and Feinberg, MPI) (Funding support, p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (Declaration of competing interest, p. 4).
funding.affiliations_note: Three authors from RTI International and one from West Virginia University. The analysis extends the authors' own baseline report (Zibbell et al., 2024), and the introduction cites an earlier FTS study with the last author (Peiper et al., 2019) for the benefit of testing. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who use drugs followed with high retention in markets with different degrees of fentanyl saturation, recording at each wave test-strip supply, contact with services, reasons for testing or not testing and what people did after each result, with overdose as an outcome, would show whether falling use reflects market saturation, supply or disengagement, and whether testing matters for overdose.

domains.note: Many measured characteristics are adjusted for, but likely common causes of witnessing overdoses, housing and FTS use are not measured: how often people used the syringe services programmes, whether they were given strips, social networks and perceived risk. Possible mediators (opioid preference, drug use) are adjusted in the same model. For the decline over waves, changes in test-strip supply or distribution are not described.

Witnessing an overdose, housing and drug use are self-reported over 6- or 30-day windows in the same interview as the outcome; reported heroin use may not mean heroin in a fentanyl-dominated market, as the authors suggest.

Convenience recruitment at two programmes where FTS are presumably obtained; the complete-case analysis keeps only the 212 who completed both follow-ups, who differed from those lost in FTS use and witnessed overdoses.
What the programmes offered after an overdose was witnessed, or during follow-up (strips, naloxone, outreach), is not described; repeated surveys about FTS may themselves prompt use.

213 of 541 (39.4%) had no follow-up and only 212 (39.2%) completed both; those lost had less lifetime FTS use and fewer witnessed overdoses. The full-sample mixed model assumes data missing at random, and the complete-case analysis (described as assumed missing at random) needs stronger assumptions, so neither addresses dropout related to unobserved FTS use; the bias most likely makes the decline look smaller, and its effect on the associations cannot be predicted.
Past-30-day FTS use is self-reported, unverified, by people recruited at services that promote testing, in the same survey as the exposures.

No registration or analysis plan; two analytic samples and interaction models, with three significant gender differences reported among many tests; the wave-specific prevalence of the outcome and the interaction estimates are not in the main text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used because the paper estimates associations of exposures (witnessing an overdose, housing, drug use) and of time with FTS use; no intervention is compared. The overall judgment follows the worst domains (unmeasured confounding by service contact and strip supply; heavy attrition related to the outcome). Citable for: in this rural cohort of people who inject drugs, the odds of past-30-day FTS use were lower at 12 months than at baseline, not at 6 months; FTS use was associated with having witnessed an overdose, heroin use and stable housing; lifetime use kept rising while recent use fell. Not citable for: reasons for the decline, a motivating effect of witnessing overdoses, how many people used FTS at each wave, any effect of testing on behaviour or overdose, or generalisation beyond people in contact with these two programmes.

key_findings.finding: Design and flow: 541 people who inject drugs completed a baseline survey (June 2021 to March 2022) at two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia; 328 completed at least one follow-up at 6 or 12 months and 212 completed both (complete-case sample); the models used 1081 observations from 541 people and 636 from 212.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results › Descriptive findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, past-30-day FTS use: lower at 12 months than at baseline in the full sample (aOR 0.642, 95% CI 0.447–0.923) and in complete cases (0.557, 0.364–0.853); no difference at 6 months (0.936, 0.696–1.258; 0.946, 0.650–1.375).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The proportion of participants using FTS at each wave is not given in the main text (descriptive statistics at all waves are in the unread supplement).

key_findings.finding: Witnessing an overdose in the past 6 months was associated with higher odds of past-30-day FTS use: aOR 2.444 (1.784–3.347) in the full sample and 2.257 (1.529–3.334) in complete cases. Among complete cases, 69.8% reported witnessing an overdose at baseline, 62.3% at 6 months and 65.1% at 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Descriptive findings, 2nd paragraph (p. 2); Model results, 2nd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Being currently unhoused was associated with lower odds of FTS use (aOR 0.679, 0.504–0.913; complete cases 0.611, 0.410–0.909), and being married or living as married with higher odds (1.521, 1.084–2.134; 1.608, 1.073–2.410). Later enrolment was associated with less use in the full sample (aOR per quarter 0.793, 0.674–0.932), not in complete cases (0.825, 0.670–1.015).

Past-30-day heroin use was associated with higher odds of FTS use (aOR 1.615, 1.107–2.357; complete cases 1.891, 1.178–3.036). No association with past-30-day fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948–1.872; 1.357, 0.879–2.095), access to heroin not containing fentanyl (0.989, 0.734–1.331; 1.157, 0.778–1.721) or own overdose in the past 6 months (0.981, 0.676–1.424; 0.712, 0.416–1.218). Preferring fentanyl over heroin: 0.775 (0.564–1.067) in the full sample and 0.662 (0.440–0.996) in complete cases.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Complete cases over time: own overdose in the prior 6 months reported by 22% at both follow-ups; preference for heroin over fentanyl fell from 58.5% at baseline to 49.1% at 6 months and 40.1% at 12 months, preference for fentanyl over heroin rose from 6.6% to 26.4% at 12 months; lifetime FTS use rose from 65.1% at baseline to 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months.

Gender: estimates did not differ by gender except in three respects: women had a greater reduction in FTS use over time than men (p < 0.05 at both follow-up waves); the negative association with fentanyl preference was stronger among men (p < 0.05); and the heroin-use estimate was higher among men (p < 0.01 full sample, p < 0.001 complete cases). The interaction estimates themselves are not printed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariable marginal effects of predictors on FTS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Attrition: compared with the complete-case sample, the 213 participants with no follow-up had less often witnessed an overdose (56.8% against 69.8%) and less often used FTS (54.3% against 65.1%), and were less likely to be married; the authors note possible bias if those lost differed systematically and that the convenience sample from two rural programmes may not generalise.

The authors interpret the decline as reflecting the reduced informational value of testing for fentanyl once its presence is expected, not unwillingness to check drugs; suggest FTS may now serve people dependent on fentanyl to confirm a purchase is fentanyl and avoid withdrawal; and call for strips that detect xylazine and medetomidine and for comprehensive community drug checking. None of these explanations was measured in the study.

reporting_issues.issue: For the complete-case sample the text gives 91% non-Hispanic White and 69% with at least a high school education, but Table 1 gives non-White race 38 of 212 (17.9%) and a high school degree for 193 (91%); the text's 91% matches the table's education figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The race and education make-up of the complete-case sample is uncertain; neither figure should be cited without this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Table 1 shows baseline descriptive statistics, but several complete-case figures equal the values the text gives for 12 months, not baseline: witnessed an overdose 65.1% (text: 69.8% at baseline, 65.1% at 12 months), preferring fentanyl over heroin 26.4% (text: 6.6% at baseline, 26.4% at 12 months), own overdose 21.7% (text: 22% at follow-up).
reporting_issues.consequence: The complete-case column cannot be read as baseline data; differences between the two columns (for example past-30-day heroin use 71% against 44.8%) may mix survey waves.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion refers to declines in FTS use at six and 12 months, but the 6-month odds ratios are 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375).
The Methods say Table 1 displays the direction and significance of the gender-stratified results; it does not, and the interaction estimates are only in the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three gender differences reported in the Results cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says fentanyl preference was associated with FTS use in the complete-case sample only, without the direction (lower odds, 0.662), and then that opioid preference does not appear to influence adoption of FTS, although the complete-case estimate and the stronger negative association among men point the other way.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that opioid preference does not matter is not supported by the paper's own estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Enrolment timing (quarters since Q2 2021) is a covariate in Table 1 but is not in the Methods' list of covariates.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the model specification is incompletely described.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1–4 (journal version, Short Report, International Journal of Drug Policy 154 (2026) 105349, available online 29 May 2026), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Fentanyl-and-analogues/rickson_2026_SouthAtlanticFTSLongitudinal.pdf: all text, Table 1 (checked on the rendered page), funding, CRediT, competing-interest and acknowledgement statements, reference list. The online supplementary material (gender-interaction models, descriptive statistics at all waves, attrition) was not read, nor the baseline paper (Zibbell et al., 2024).
